extracted.intended_audience: USPTO personnel and stakeholders (e.g., patent examiners and practitioners) evaluating subject-matter eligibility of AI-related patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the USPTO/MPEP subject-matter eligibility (SME) analysis to patent claims, with examples focused on AI inventions (new examples 47–49). Covers Step 1, Step 2A (Prong One and Prong Two), and Step 2B analysis and claim interpretation under the MPEP flowchart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow MPEP 2106 flowchart for SME analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the flowchart in MPEP 2106, subsection III, to determine whether a claim satisfies the criteria for subject matter eligibility and to organize the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The slides indicate examiners should follow the flowchart when analyzing claims (Step 1, Step 2A Prong One, Step 2A Prong Two, Step 2B). The examples are analyzed using that flowchart. Following the flowchart will help organize thoughts when analyzing a claim for subject matter eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category test
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim falls within at least one statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites an integrated circuit it is a machine/manufacture; if it recites a series of steps it is a process. Step 1 must be answered Yes to proceed to further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — identify judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify specific claim limitation(s) that you believe recite a judicial exception and determine whether those limitation(s) fall within the abstract idea groupings enumerated in MPEP 2106.04(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-part evaluation: (a) identify the limitation(s) alleged to be an abstract idea; (b) determine if the limitation falls within mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity. Claims that merely involve an exception but do not recite one may be eligible and not require further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping — Mathematical Concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that recite optimization algorithms, backpropagation, gradient descent, arithmetic calculations, or other explicit mathematical computation fall into this grouping. Example: training using backpropagation and gradient descent is treated as mathematical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping — Mental Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts performed in the human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim steps that encompass mental choices, evaluations, observing data sets, identifying anomalies, or comparing scores against thresholds may be treated as mental processes. Example: 'discretizing' or 'detecting' or 'analyzing' anomalies can encompass mental process abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping — Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes fundamental economic principles or practices (hedging, insurance, mitigating risk), commercial or legal interactions (agreements, contracts, advertising, marketing, sales), and managing personal behavior or relationships (social activities, teaching, following rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this grouping when claim limitations relate to business practices, legal/commercial interactions, or interpersonal management activities as enumerated in MPEP 2106.04(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — limitations indicative of integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify additional elements beyond a judicial exception and evaluate whether they integrate the exception into a practical application (making the claim more than an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations indicative of integration include: improvements to the functioning of a computer or other technology/technical field (MPEP 2106.05(a)); applying/using an exception to effect a particular treatment/prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition (MPEP 2106.04(d)(2)); applying the judicial exception with/by use of a particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)); effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (MPEP 2106.05(c)); applying/using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a technological environment such that the claim as a whole is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the exception (MPEP 2106.04(d)(2) and 2106.05(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — limitations not indicative of integration (insignificant extra-solution activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claim recitations do not show integration into a practical application and are not sufficient to render an abstract idea patent eligible at Step 2A Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer; merely using a computer as a tool; adding insignificant extra-solution activity; generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Note: Step 2A Prong Two does NOT include the 'well understood, routine, conventional' (WURC) consideration—WURC is considered only in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — inventive concept and WURC consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim provides an inventive concept (i.e., additional element(s) or combination that amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception), adding consideration of whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2B includes the considerations from Step 2A plus WURC (MPEP 2106.05(d)). Limitations indicative of an inventive concept include improvements to computer functioning or other technology (MPEP 2106.05(a)), applying the exception with/by particular machine (MPEP 2106.05(b)), effecting a transformation (MPEP 2106.05(c)), applying the exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linking (MPEP 2106.04(d)(2) & 2106.05(e)), and adding a specific limitation that is not well-understood, routine, or conventional (MPEP 2106.05(d)). Limitations not indicative include appending WURC activities, adding 'apply it' or insignificant extra-solution activity, or mere linking to a technological environment (MPEP 2106.05(f),(g),(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim terms under the broadest reasonable interpretation standard when establishing the claim scope for SME analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI examples given: 'continuous data' = any data measured with many possible values; 'discretizing' includes binning, clustering, rounding; backpropagation/gradient descent treated as optimization/mathematical calculations. Do not disregard limitations (a 'wherein' clause has weight); consider the plain meaning and specification when evaluating whether claim language limits the scope (e.g., specifying 'Compound X eye drops' imparts patentable weight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception versus those that merely 'involve' it
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to distinguish claims that actually recite a judicial exception (which require further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception but do not recite it (which may be eligible without further analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Supreme Court guidance: '[a]t some level, all inventions embody, use, reflect, rest upon, or apply laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas.' Examiners should carefully determine whether a claim recites an exception or merely involves it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples cautiously; case-by-case analysis; no fixed keyword list
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (including examples 47–49) are illustrative only and should be interpreted based on their fact patterns; there is no fixed list of terms that render a claim eligible or ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary for a claim to mirror an example claim to be eligible. Older examples may be inconsistent with current guidance and should be used with caution. Every claim must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis using MPEP SME guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate alleged 'extra-solution' activities and routine laboratory techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether data-gathering or laboratory steps are merely insignificant extra-solution activity and whether laboratory techniques are well-known, routine, and conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: collecting/genotyping a sample can be 'mere data gathering' and, if the laboratory technique is recognized as routine (e.g., analyzing DNA to detect allelic variants), it may be considered well-understood, routine, conventional activity under Step 2B and not supply an inventive concept. Re-evaluate extra-solution activity in Step 2B with WURC in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical-improvement requirement for considering 'using' an ANN or computer as more than generic
rubrics_metrics.description: To conclude a claim improves computer functioning or technology (and thus integrates the exception), the specification and claim must present a technical explanation of the asserted improvement and the claim must reflect that improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely 'using' an ANN or computer at a high level of generality amounts to instructions to implement the exception on a generic computer and will not, by itself, establish eligibility. The claim/specification must show how the claimed elements effect a technological improvement (e.g., real-time remediation as an actual technical improvement rather than a stated outcome).
